title: Ordinary trace in a finite-dimensional exact sequence
statement: Let $k$ be a field and $A,B,C$ finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Let $i:A\to B$ and $q:B\to C$ be linear maps with $i$ injective, $q$ surjective and $\operatorname{im}(i)=\ker(q)$. For linear endomorphisms $f_A,f_B,f_C$ satisfying $f_Bi=if_A$ and $qf_B=f_Cq$, ordinary trace [def-weil-endomorphism-trace] satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(f_B\mid B)=\operatorname{tr}(f_A\mid A)+\operatorname{tr}(f_C\mid C)$.

source.place: §1, pp. 149–150, (T1) and the finite-dimensional case of (T2)

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-projective], the $k$-vector space $C$ is projective. Apply the lifting characterization in [def-weil-pbc-projective-module] to the surjection $q:B\to C$ and the linear map $1_C:C\to C$. It gives a $k$-linear map $s:C\to B$ with $qs=1_C$. No compatibility between $s$ and the endomorphisms is asserted.

source.place: Tag 05CE (definition-projective), the Hom-exactness/lifting characterization preceding Tag 05CF (lemma-characterize-projective); projectivity over a field from Tag 09FN (fields-lemma-vector-space-is-free)

proof.text: For $b\in B$, $q(b-sq(b))=q(b)-qsq(b)=0$. Exactness and injectivity of $i$ therefore give a unique $r(b)\in A$ satisfying $i(r(b))=b-sq(b)$. This defines a linear map $r:B\to A$: applying $i$ to $r(b+b^{\prime})$ and to $r(b)+r(b^{\prime})$ gives the same vector, and applying $i$ to $r(\lambda b)$ and to $\lambda r(b)$ gives the same vector; injectivity gives the two linearity identities. Moreover $qi=0$ by exactness, so $i(r(i(a)))=i(a)-sq(i(a))=i(a)$ and hence $ri=1_A$. The defining identity also gives $ir+sq=1_B$. These are identities of linear maps, obtained pointwise.

source.place: §1, p. 150, (T2), ordinary finite-dimensional case; omitted linear-algebra argument supplied by Q16

proof.text: The matrix definition of trace [def-weil-endomorphism-trace] gives additivity: in a single finite basis of $B$, the diagonal entries of the matrix of $u+v$ are the sums of those of $u$ and $v$, so summing them gives $\operatorname{tr}_B(u+v)=\operatorname{tr}_B(u)+\operatorname{tr}_B(v)$. Apply this to $f_B=f_B(ir+sq)=(f_Bi)r+(f_Bs)q$, obtaining $\operatorname{tr}_B(f_B)=\operatorname{tr}_B((f_Bi)r)+\operatorname{tr}_B((f_Bs)q)$.

source.place: §1, p. 150, (T2), ordinary finite-dimensional case; omitted linear-algebra argument supplied by Q16

proof.text: Apply [lem-pc-finite-dimensional-trace-cyclic] first to the maps $r:B\to A$ and $f_Bi:A\to B$, and then to $q:B\to C$ and $f_Bs:C\to B$. All spaces involved are finite-dimensional by the hypotheses of the item. The two summands from the preceding step become $\operatorname{tr}_A(rf_Bi)$ and $\operatorname{tr}_C(qf_Bs)$, respectively.

source.place: §1, p. 150, (T2), ordinary finite-dimensional case; omitted linear-algebra argument supplied by Q16

proof.text: Use the assumed intertwining identities and the identities just constructed: $rf_Bi=rif_A=f_A$ because $ri=1_A$, and $qf_Bs=f_Cqs=f_C$ because $qs=1_C$. Substituting into the preceding trace equality gives $\operatorname{tr}(f_B\mid B)=\operatorname{tr}(f_A\mid A)+\operatorname{tr}(f_C\mid C)$, as required.

source.place: §1, p. 150, (T2), ordinary finite-dimensional case; omitted linear-algebra argument supplied by Q16
